Write a note to a friend about garden tools that never seem to work. Aim for about 400 words. Reply with the note only.
final_message:
Dear Walter,

You asked how the new season is going, and I will tell you plainly: the tools are winning. I bought a trowel in March that bends if you look at it sternly. It was sold to me as "forged," which I now believe to be a word of aspiration, like "unsinkable." Yesterday I put it into a patch of ordinary clay, and it folded up like a gentleman receiving bad news. I went on digging with a soup spoon from the kitchen, and the spoon, I am sorry to say, did better.

Then there is the hoe. You will remember the hoe. It has a handle of the finest ash, and a blade that was meant, I think, for some other and softer planet. It will cut a weed if the weed is willing. If the weed has any character at all, it merely leans aside, and the hoe goes by with a sort of apologetic swish. I have stood and watched a dandelion survive three strokes in a row. I took off my hat to it.

The pruning shears are the worst of the lot. They have a spring that is meant to open the jaws after each cut; but the spring has views of its own, and prefers to keep them shut. So I cut a twig, and then I must pry the shears open with my other hand, like a man releasing a small and stubborn trap. Polly says that I might oil them. I have oiled them. They are now shut with a great deal more dignity, and that is all.

I have thought of going to the shop and making a complaint; but I know exactly what would happen. The man would look at the tool, and then at me, and then say that it works perfectly well for him. And it would; that is the dreadful part. Tools, like dogs, know their masters, and mine have taken the measure of me early.

Meanwhile the garden goes on without regard to my equipment. The peas are up, the lettuce is thinking about it, and the weeds are in full and splendid health. I propose to meet them with my bare hands, which have never yet failed me, except in the matter of blisters.

Come and see us when you can, and bring your own spade. I will lend you the soup spoon.

Yours in the dirt,
[name]
